extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; historians and journalists interested in Civil War–era war reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Practices, standards, and evaluative observations about war correspondence and editorial conduct during the American Civil War (1860–1872), including dispatching, censorship, verification, and editorial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: “Published reports from the front were very commonly three or four days old, and sometimes much older.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telegraph facilities were limited or unavailable; correspondents sometimes rode long distances or carried stories personally to telegraph offices. Wires could be refused for government, military censorship, or commercial reasons; breaks in service caused delay. Assess wartime reporting by how it managed these logistical constraints and how clearly it labeled the currency of its information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of rumor (‘grapevine telegraph’)
rubrics_metrics.description: “‘Grapevine telegraph’— slang for rumor— played an important part in news communication during the war. The heading ‘important— if true’ was common in all papers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers frequently published unverified reports (e.g., columns titled 'rumors and speculations'). Rumor was stimulated by inefficient censorship; newspapers often became victims of lies and canards. Good practice: flag unverified items, avoid treating rumor as fact, and attempt verification before amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-writing style and leads
rubrics_metrics.description: “The modern news-story lead had not yet been developed, but news writing was more direct than in ante-bellum days.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official reports were often printed in full rather than being summarized; dispatches tended to be printed chronologically with the oldest at the head. When evaluating period war copy, note the absence of contemporary lead conventions and the reliance on direct, unabridged official material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and format of dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dispatches were likely to be printed chronologically, the oldest at the head of the column. Following the story of a battle, there would be the long list of killed, wounded, and missing, in small type.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect battlefield columns to include chronological dispatch aggregation and casualty lists appended in condensed typesetting. These formatting norms shaped reader comprehension and should be judged for clarity and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of maps and pictorials
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great newspapers occasionally published war maps; this was a type of enterprise in which the Philadelphia Inquirer and the New York Herald were leaders... The two great pictorials— Harper’s Weekly and Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper— each had sometimes as many as a dozen artists in the field drawing pictures— sometimes under fire— for reproduction by woodcuts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations and maps were valuable explanatory aids; their presence indicates editorial investment in battlefield orientation and reader service. Assess the quality, accuracy, and timeliness of such visual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary sourcing: special correspondents vs bureaus and reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: “Only the largest papers could afford to keep special correspondents in the field. The others got their news from their Washington bureaus, from the Associated Press, or second-hand from other papers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate coverage by source: firsthand ‘specials’ provided eye-witness accounts; bureaus/AP handled distribution; many smaller weeklies supplemented with letters from officers and privates. Transparency about sourcing and attribution is a key quality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status, risks, and noncombatant recognition of correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: “Special correspondents in the field representing individual papers (‘specials,’ they were called for short) were not recognized as noncombatants. They were quite as liable to attack by the enemy... Some were killed in action, some wounded, and some captured.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters operated with battlefield risk and without assured noncombatant status; assess safety practices, attachments to staffs, and how reporting duties exposed them to danger. Consider ethical implications of embedding and the physical risks accepted to secure eyewitness reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondent enterprise, stamina, and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Profiles of correspondents (e.g., Coffin, Reid, Villard, Richardson) emphasize 'powers of toil,' topographical skill, honesty, and willingness to ride long distances to verify reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality war reporting required physical endurance, initiative (riding long distances, penetrating lines), technical skills (surveying, topography), social skills (gaining commanders' confidence), and a commitment to verification. These personal attributes functioned as de facto performance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and skepticism over rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show correspondents 'placing no trust in mere rumors' and undertaking long journeys to 'probe a report which was important if true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice demanded active verification of reports—investigating rumors rather than publishing them as fact. Anti-pattern: publishing speculative reports without corroboration, which could mislead public opinion and military planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding publication of military secrets / compliance with censorship rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the 57th Article of War (court-martial for giving military information to the enemy) and a General Order forbidding printing of any news of camps, troops, or military or naval movements except by permission of the general in command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors faced legal/military constraints: publishing troop movements or sensitive military information risked harming operations and could incur severe penalties. Best practice balanced press freedom with responsibility for national security; many outlets negotiated informal or formal restrictions with military authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraphic censorship and control of transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the telegraph lines from Washington, including most of the strategic lines, were placed under censors of the State Department in April, 1861... This censorship was administered under inadequate rules... The censorship was later taken over by the War Department and an assistant secretary made 'military superintendent of all telegraphic lines and offices in the United States.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how telegraphic control affected news flow: strategic lines were censored, causing delays and inconsistencies. Reporters had to navigate or circumvent censors; newspapers needed policies for dealing with delayed, held, or redacted dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial self-censorship and newsroom-imposed restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: “The better correspondents... used much skill in concealing information of value to the enemy; generally they were as devoted to the Union cause as any soldier. Editors, too, imposed their censorship, and some exercised very great care in such matters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms often practiced internal censorship to avoid endangering troops or aiding the enemy. Assess editorial judgment regarding what to withhold, and whether internal restraints respected both public information needs and military security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of correspondents becoming press agents (loss of objectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A real abuse resulted from the efforts of the correspondents to cultivate the favor of the generals in command... ‘Specials’ thus became press agents for their generals and built up popular and even political reputations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivating personal favor with commanders compromised independence and could produce promotional or partisan reporting. Anti-patterns include puffing, undue advocacy for particular generals, and failure to maintain critical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial criticism and the role of the press as 'arm-chair generals'
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never was there a war in which arm-chair generalship from newspaper offices was more vociferous, in which more editors became military strategists over night.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often pronounced strategy and criticized commanders; this influenced public opinion and sometimes policy. When evaluating editorial conduct, consider whether criticism was informed, responsible, and mindful of its potential impact on morale and operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home-office organization of war coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never before had newspapers organized the coverage of a war from their home offices. That, however, is precisely what the great northern papers were forced to do... ”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective wartime journalism required centralized planning and coordination (Washington bureaus, desks organizing dispatches, editorial policies). Evaluate the degree of organization, allocation of resources (e.g., number of 'specials'), and editorial systems for integrating field reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of by-lines and pen-names
rubrics_metrics.description: “Early in the conflict the War Department... requested papers to use by-lines in connection with their publication of war stories. This device had one effect not contemplated: it made the pen names of many war 'specials' famous.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution practices affected correspondent anonymity, fame, and risk. Assess by-line policies for their effects on safety, accountability, and the creation of celebrity correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between freedom of the press and military secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Freedom of the press beyond anything ever before known in the world had become a fixed national tradition... Under the stress of military conditions, the administration felt that some restrictions were necessary... but there was no consistent enforcement of any fixed body of rules controlling the press.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was a persistent conflict: censorship could restrain 'wholesome discussion and criticism' while unchecked reporting could imperil operations. Evaluate reporting against this tension—did coverage responsibly balance public interest and national security?

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of inaccurate or premature reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes (e.g., Raymond’s premature dispatch about Bull Run) show that incomplete or censored dispatches could lead to false public impressions and competitive editorial consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess journalistic practices for managing partial information, the risks of publishing premature victory or defeat reports, and newsroom mechanisms (e.g., holding copy, verification) used to mitigate harm from incorrect dispatches.
